# On the Strange Gift of Noticing

I want to talk about attention. Not the kind that gets weaponized in social media algorithms or hoarded by the entertainment industry, though those are real problems. I mean something simpler and stranger: the basic human capacity to notice things, and what happens when you actually do it.

We move through the world mostly asleep. I don't mean this as criticism—it's necessary. If you genuinely paid attention to everything, you'd be paralyzed. The texture of your socks, the sound of your refrigerator, the seventeen aches in your body, the implications of climate change, the fact that everyone around you will die, the dust motes floating through the air: conscious attention to all of this simultaneously would break your mind. So we have a filter. We have a default setting that lets us operate on autopilot, noticing only what our brain has deemed important or novel or threatening.

But here's what I've become obsessed with lately: sometimes that filter breaks, or you deliberately break it, and the world becomes almost violently interesting.

I experienced this recently on an ordinary Tuesday morning. I was waiting for a coffee at my usual café—a place I've been hundreds of times—and I actually *looked* at the barista's hands. Not in a weird way. Just looked. Really looked. Her hands were making a cappuccino, moving with the kind of unconscious grace that comes from doing something ten thousand times. She was texturing the milk, and her movements were small, precise, almost musical. The way her fingers held the pitcher, the subtle angle of her wrist, the exact moment when the foam started to form: these were small masterpieces of motor control, developed through years of repetition, but also something more than that. There was intelligence in those hands. Actual knowledge that couldn't be articulated, only demonstrated.

I'd seen her make coffee five hundred times before. But I'd never *watched* her make coffee until that Tuesday.

The experience was oddly moving. Not because anything special happened—it was just a cappuccino—but because I'd suddenly accessed a layer of reality that had been there all along, invisible in its ordinariness. It made me think about how many invisible masterpieces I walk past every day. How many small perfections of practiced skill and embodied knowledge are operating constantly around me, unwitnessed because I'm too busy, too distracted, too much in my own head.

This is what I mean about noticing. It's not about being mindful in that sanitized, yoga-class sense where you're trying to optimize your experience or find inner peace or whatever. It's something more basic than that. It's about the fact that reality is almost infinitely textured and interesting if you can break the filter long enough to see it.

Writers have always understood this. That's a lot of what writing is: training yourself to notice. I think about Proust spending pages describing the sensation of a madeleine cookie dissolving on his tongue, or Annie Dillard writing an entire chapter about how light moves through a prism, and I recognize what they're doing. They're saying: stop. Look at this. This ordinary thing contains the entire world if you know how to see it.

The problem is that modern life is specifically engineered to prevent this kind of attention. We're in an arms race between our attention and everything designed to capture it. Apps use slot-machine mechanics to keep you scrolling. News feeds are optimized for outrage. Every website is trying to sell you something. Television commercials interrupt narratives to interrupt your mind. And this is all on top of just the normal chaos of being alive—bills, work, relationships, the basic effort of getting through the day without falling apart.

No wonder we're all numb. No wonder we walk past beauty without seeing it. The machinery is too loud.

But I think there's something to be said for fighting back, even in small ways. Even in ways that feel quaintly useless against the machinery.

Last week I decided to take a different route on my morning walk. Same neighborhood, just different streets. I've lived here for three years and I realized I'd never actually been down Elm Street, which runs parallel to my normal route. It's maybe two blocks long. And in those two blocks, I saw: a magnificent old oak tree growing through what looked like someone's entire front garden, twisted and gnarled like something from a fairy tale; a hand-painted sign on someone's fence that said "BEWARE: TERRITORIAL SQUIRREL" (presumably serious); the most elaborate and slightly unhinged garden gnome collection I've ever witnessed, easily two dozen gnomes arranged in what appeared to be an apocalyptic diorama; and a woman sitting on her porch at 6 AM reading a physical book and drinking something steaming from a mug, and she looked up and we made eye contact and smiled at each other like we'd recognized something.

All of this was two blocks from my house. Two blocks I'd never walked down before because I was on autopilot, following the same path, seeing the same things, my attention elsewhere.

This is one of the genuine mysteries of consciousness that nobody really talks about: how much of the world you fail to see because you're not paying attention. It's not hidden or secret. It's just there, in plain sight, waiting to be noticed. The difference between a familiar street and a magical street is just the quality of attention you bring to it.

I think about this a lot in the context of relationships too. There's this moment that happens with people you love, where you suddenly see them instead of just looking at them. Maybe it's accidental—the light hits their face a certain way while they're concentrating on something, and you notice the exact shade of their eyes, or a line around their mouth that wasn't there last year, or the way they bite their lip when they're thinking. And suddenly they're not just a familiar person who you've integrated into your daily life on autopilot; they're a specific human being, with a specific body and face and presence that you're actually choosing to perceive.

These moments of genuine seeing usually trigger something in me. Sometimes it's tenderness. Sometimes it's sadness—the recognition that this person is real and mortal and will someday die and I will miss them. Sometimes it's just a deeper connection, like actually *meeting* them instead of just coexisting.

But they're rarer than they should be.

I think a lot of relationship problems come down to this failure to see each other. We get used to someone and they become part of the furniture of our lives. We stop looking. They become a collection of habits and patterns instead of an actual person. And then we wonder why it feels like we're drifting apart.

What if the antidote to that is just... looking? Actually looking at the person you love and trying to see them, really see them, the way you might see a stranger whose face catches your attention?

This might sound exhausting. And in a way it is—genuine attention is effortful. But it's also the opposite of exhausting in a deeper sense. The things that usually exhaust us are the things we're doing on autopilot, halfheartedly, while thinking about something else. Like you're pushing a boulder uphill with only half your attention, so it keeps rolling back. Whereas when you genuinely pay attention to something, when you're fully present, there's a strange energy that comes with it. Time slows down. Things become vivid. You feel more awake.

I've started experimenting with this deliberately. Not in a self-help way where I'm supposed to be "present" and achieve some optimal mental state. Just occasionally breaking my autopilot and actually looking at things.

I'll be on the subway and instead of my default state—earbuds in, phone out, mentally elsewhere—I'll just watch people. Not in a creepy surveillance way, but with genuine curiosity about their specific human-ness. The teenager with the specific way of slumping that contains an entire attitude. The older woman with the shopping bag and perfect posture and tired eyes that suggest several decades of a story I'll never know. The guy with the specific combination of facial hair and fashion choices that represents a deliberate choice to present himself in this particular way to the world.

Everyone is so specific. Everyone is solving a unique set of problems and has a unique way of moving through the world. Once you start noticing this, it's hard to go back to seeing people as generic background characters in your own story.

Or I'll sit in a coffee shop and actually pay attention to the light. How it moves. How it changes. How it hits different surfaces differently. How it's never the same from one moment to the next, even though you think of light as constant. A photographer understands this; they're trained to see light. But most of us just take it for granted, like it's just a utility that keeps us from bumping into things.

But light is beautiful. Genuinely. If you look at it.

I wonder sometimes if what we call boredom is actually just the state of being present without the proper attention to notice anything interesting. Like if you're stuck in traffic, most people feel bored because they're imprisoned in a car with nothing to do. But if you brought the quality of attention you'd bring to a nature documentary to the traffic jam—the way the car ahead of you moves, the specific combination of sounds and smells, the micro-interactions with other drivers, the stories those other cars contain—would it still be boring? Or would it become interesting?

I'm not sure this is a profound insight. It might be that I'm just describing the placebo effect, or finding interest in things because I've decided in advance to find them interesting. Maybe there's no real difference.

But there does seem to be something qualitatively different about a life where you're actually paying attention versus one where you're just going through the motions. The people I know who seem happiest, who seem most alive, seem to have access to this capacity to notice. They find the strange beauty in ordinary things. They actually *see* the people they love. They're not constantly checked out, running their internal monologue about something else.

And the people I know who seem most depressed or numb seem to have the inverse problem. Everything has become a gray blur. Nothing is interesting because they've stopped looking.

I don't think the solution is just "pay more attention." That's too simple and also a little bit cruel to say to someone who's depressed. Depression rewires your attention in ways that aren't under your conscious control. But I do think there's something to the idea that attention and vitality are connected.

Last night I was walking home at dusk, that strange in-between time when it's not quite dark but not quite light, and the sky was this color I don't think I have a word for. Not quite purple, not quite blue, with some kind of rose tone mixed in. And the trees were silhouetted against it, and the streetlights were starting to come on and creating these little pools of yellow. And I just stopped walking for a moment and stared at it.

It was a completely ordinary dusk. This is something that happens every single day. But I noticed it. And in noticing it, I felt something shift inside me. A recognition of beauty. A sudden acute awareness of the fact that I'm alive and able to perceive this and that this will happen again tomorrow and I'll probably miss it again tomorrow because I'll be thinking about something else.

But at least I saw it once.

I think that's worth something. I think in a world that's increasingly designed to make us numb and distracted and profitable, the act of actually paying attention to something is almost radical. It's saying that this moment matters, that the ordinary world contains something worth seeing, that your experience right now is not something to endure but something to actually inhabit.

It's free, which is one reason why it matters so much. The machinery can't profit off your attention if you're paying attention to dusk or light or the specific way someone you love moves their hands. The attention you give to the real world is not monetizable. It's not valuable in any economic sense. It's valuable only in the sense that a life full of noticed moments feels richer than a life of unconscious motion.

So I'm going to keep doing this. I'm going to keep looking at things. I'm going to keep breaking the autopilot whenever I can manage it. I'm going to keep noticing the small masterpieces of ordinary life that nobody's trying to see anymore because there's so much competing noise.

And I'm going to suggest that you try it too, whenever you get a chance. Look at something. Really look. Notice something you've been walking past. See someone you've been taking for granted. Pay attention to the light.

The world is still here. It's still strange and beautiful and full of specific textures and details. It's just waiting for you to notice it.
